# Testing Data Analysis Workflows {#sec-testing} Your script reads a length-of-stay column from an institutional warehouse, and one quarter the warehouse begins reporting it in seconds where it previously reported days. Nothing errors. The column is still numeric, the join still succeeds, the model still fits, and every downstream number is wrong by a factor of 86,400. No amount of rereading your code will find the problem, because your code is not what changed. A one-line test asserting that length of stay falls in a plausible range fails on the first run after the change; this chapter is about writing that line, and about finding out whether the tests you already have would notice anything at all. ::: {.bookepigraph} ```{=latex} \begin{flushright}\small ``` *Program testing can be used to show the presence of bugs, but never to show their absence.* [Edsger W. Dijkstra]{.smallcaps}, *Notes on Structured Programming* (1970) ```{=latex} \end{flushright} ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Where this chapter sits: tests belong to the Analyze stage, beside the code they check, and run again every time the code or the data change.](20-testing_files/figure-html/fig-testing-pipeline-1.png){#fig-testing-pipeline fig-align='center' fig-alt='Diagram of the analysis pipeline: six stages in order (Plan, Acquire, Wrangle, Analyze, Report, Share) above two bands that run under every stage (Version control and Environment). Highlighted for this chapter: Analyze.' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note title='In this chapter'} **Reading time.** About 30 minutes. **You'll need.** @sec-wrangling for the `dplyr` verbs and @sec-types for dates and coded values. The code uses: ```r library(tinytest) library(palmerpenguins) ``` and calls `dplyr`, `tidyr`, and `janitor` with their namespaces. **You'll be able to.** - Write `tinytest` unit tests that assert values, boundaries, and errors, not only the shape of the output. - Build a small fixture that exercises every branch of a cleaning function, and pair it with an integration test on the real file. - Show that a test suite would catch a bug by planting one (mutation testing). - Run the suite in continuous integration so that a failing test fails the build. **Outline.** - [Why test an analysis](#sec-testing-why) - [Unit tests with tinytest](#sec-testing-unit) - [Structure versus correctness](#sec-testing-correctness) - [Test smells](#sec-testing-smells) - [Worked example: testing the HF-HOME CRF cleaner](#sec-testing-worked) - [Running tests in continuous integration](#sec-testing-ci) - [For testthat readers](#sec-testing-testthat) ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Skip ahead?'} If these answers come quickly, skip to the next chapter. The answers are in @sec-quiz-answers-20. 1. Why would you test a one-off data analysis script that will only ever run on a single dataset? 2. What is the difference between a unit test, an integration test, and an end-to-end test in the context of a data analysis pipeline? 3. What does `tinytest::expect_equal_to_reference()` capture, and when is a reference test preferable to a direct value-comparison test? ::: ## Why test an analysis {#sec-testing-why} Analysis code rarely gets tested, and the reason is a respectable one. Software is written to run on inputs its author has never seen; an analysis script is written to run on one dataset, once. The reasoning has two holes. The script does not run once: it runs every time an extract is refreshed, an exclusion is revised, or a reviewer asks for a sensitivity analysis, and by then its author has forgotten which branches were ever exercised. And the failures that matter in analysis code do not stop it running. A filter that removes the wrong rows, a join that duplicates a patient, a unit conversion applied twice: all produce output. The question a test answers is not 'did it run' but 'would I have noticed if it were wrong', and for most analysis scripts the honest answer is no. Three ordinary occasions make the case concrete (@tbl-testing-occasions). | Occasion | What changes | What the test asserts | |---|---|---| | Refactoring | Your code, on purpose: `base::merge()` becomes a `dplyr` join | The output is identical to a saved baseline | | Upstream drift | The data, silently: days become seconds | Values fall in plausible ranges; codes are in the codebook | | Documentation | Nobody's memory of the intent | Given input X, the function returns Y, and a false claim fails the build | : Three occasions a test pays for itself. {#tbl-testing-occasions} Tests come in layers that catch different failures (@fig-test-layers). For analysis code the pyramid familiar from software engineering is flatter: the integration layer, a small synthetic dataset run through the whole pipeline, does more work here than in most applications. ```{mermaid} %%| echo: false %%| label: fig-test-layers %%| fig-alt: "Three stacked layers in increasing scope. Unit tests %%| exercise one function on known input, catch helper bugs, and %%| cost seconds. Integration tests run the whole pipeline on a %%| twenty-line synthetic dataset, catch composition bugs and %%| silent filter and join errors, and cost seconds. End-to-end %%| tests run raw data through to final figures, catch everything %%| remaining, and cost minutes to hours." %%| fig-cap: "The three test layers and what each one catches. %%| Unit tests are fast and narrow; end-to-end tests are slow and %%| broad; the integration layer, where a synthetic dataset is run %%| through the whole cleaning pipeline, has the best cost-benefit %%| ratio for analysis code and is the layer most often missing." flowchart TD U["Unit
one function, known input
catches: helper bugs
cost: seconds"] I["Integration
whole pipeline, 20-line
synthetic dataset
catches: composition bugs,
silent filter and join errors
cost: seconds"] E["End to end
raw data to final figures
catches: everything left
cost: minutes to hours"] U --> I --> E ``` ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** A cleaning script filters to adults with `filter(age >= 18)`. Six months later someone discovers that the export encodes unknown age as `-1`, so those rows were silently dropped as minors. Which layer would have caught it, and what would the test have asserted? **Answer.** The integration layer, and only if the synthetic dataset contained a `-1`. A unit test of the filter passes: given ages 17, 25, and 40 it correctly keeps two. The function is not broken; the *data* violated an assumption the function never stated. Two assertions are worth writing, and they fail at different times. One on the input, that `age` falls in a plausible range before the filter runs, fails the day the export changes. One on the output, that the number of rows dropped is what the codebook predicts, fails the day the meaning changes. The first is a claim about the data; the second is a claim about your understanding of it. ::: ## Unit tests with tinytest {#sec-testing-unit} The book uses `tinytest`. It has no dependencies of its own, which matters when the surrounding chapters are about pinning an environment; each test file runs on its own; and its assertion vocabulary is small enough to hold in your head. If you will work in a `testthat` project, @sec-testing-testthat translates. For a function in `R/clean.R`: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} #' Compute age groups from numeric age #' @param age numeric vector age_group <- function(age) { cut(age, breaks = c(0, 18, 40, 65, Inf), right = FALSE, labels = c("under-18", "18-39", "40-64", "65+")) } ``` ::: Tests in `inst/tinytest/test-clean.R`: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tinytest) expect_equal(as.character(age_group(c(20, 50, 75))), c("18-39", "40-64", "65+"), info = "typical adult ages bin correctly") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_equal(as.character(age_group(c(20, 50, 75))), c("18-39", #> call| "40-64", "65+"), info = "typical adult ages bin correctly") #> info| typical adult ages bin correctly # the interval starts are inclusive, because right = FALSE expect_equal(as.character(age_group(c(18, 40, 65))), c("18-39", "40-64", "65+"), info = "boundary values fall in the upper bin") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_equal(as.character(age_group(c(18, 40, 65))), c("18-39", #> call| "40-64", "65+"), info = "boundary values fall in the upper bin") #> info| boundary values fall in the upper bin expect_equal(as.character(age_group(c(17, 39, 64))), c("under-18", "18-39", "40-64"), info = "values just below a break stay below") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_equal(as.character(age_group(c(17, 39, 64))), c("under-18", #> call| "18-39", "40-64"), info = "values just below a break stay below") #> info| values just below a break stay below # NA_real_, not NA: bare NA is logical, and cut() rejects it. The # distinction is invisible until the test is actually run. expect_true(is.na(age_group(NA_real_)), info = "numeric NA propagates rather than erroring") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_true(is.na(age_group(NA)), info = "numeric NA propagates rather than erroring") #> info| numeric NA propagates rather than erroring expect_error(age_group("twenty"), info = "non-numeric input is rejected") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_error(age_group("twenty"), info = "non-numeric input is rejected") #> info| non-numeric input is rejected ``` ::: Each `expect_*()` call is one test, and its `info=` string says what it checks; a failure reports the file and line beside it. The tests above follow the rule that edge cases are where bugs live: boundaries, missing values, and the wrong type. For other functions the list includes empty input, a single observation, a group with one member, zero variance, and perfect collinearity. Run every test file from the project root, or a package's tests by name (display-only; both need a project with an `inst/tinytest/` directory): ```r tinytest::test_all() tinytest::test_package("practicum") ``` `tinytest` expects the test files in `inst/tinytest/` and a one-line `tests/tinytest.R` that runs them, which is the layout `tinytest::setup_tinytest()` creates and the one `zzcollab` scaffolds. Tests under `inst/` are installed with the package, so someone who has your compendium can run its tests without your source tree. For an analysis whose credibility rests on being checkable by someone else, that is the right default. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** Written as `expect_true(is.na(age_group(NA)))`, the `NA` test errors instead of passing. What does that tell you about the function, beyond the test? **Answer.** Bare `NA` is logical, and `cut()` requires a numeric argument, so `age_group(NA)` stops with `'x' must be numeric`. The same input arises in production: a column that is empty in every row is read by `read.csv()` as logical, and the function then fails on it. The test has found a real input the function does not handle, which is what a test is for. ::: ### Exercises 1. `age_group()` is tested for typical ages, boundaries, `NA`, and non-numeric input. One gap remains: what the function does with an age outside the range the breaks cover. Find the behavior, decide whether it is the behavior you want, and write the test that pins whichever answer you choose. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} as.character(age_group(c(-5, 0, 200))) #> [1] NA "under-18" "65+" ``` ::: A negative age returns `NA`, because the breaks begin at 0 and `cut()` places anything below the first break outside every interval. An age of 200 is absorbed into `65+`, because the last break is `Inf`. The asymmetry is the finding: an impossible age at the top of the range is silently accepted, and an impossible age at the bottom becomes the same `NA` a genuinely missing age produces. Pinning the current behavior: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} expect_true(is.na(age_group(-5)), info = "age below the first break gives NA") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_true(is.na(age_group(-5)), info = "age below the first break gives NA") #> info| age below the first break gives NA ``` ::: Preferring an error instead, the test comes first and the function changes to satisfy it: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} age_group_strict <- function(age) { stopifnot(is.numeric(age)) if (any(age < 0, na.rm = TRUE)) stop("negative age") cut(age, breaks = c(0, 18, 40, 65, Inf), right = FALSE, labels = c("under-18", "18-39", "40-64", "65+")) } expect_error(age_group_strict(-5), pattern = "negative age", info = "negative age is rejected") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_error(age_group_strict(-5), pattern = "negative age", #> call| info = "negative age is rejected") #> info| negative age is rejected expect_equal(as.character(age_group_strict(30)), "18-39", info = "a valid age still bins correctly") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_equal(as.character(age_group_strict(30)), "18-39", info = "a valid age still bins correctly") #> info| a valid age still bins correctly ``` ::: Either is defensible. Leaving the behavior untested is not, because then it is not a decision at all, only whatever `cut()` happened to do. ::: ## Structure versus correctness {#sec-testing-correctness} A test that the result 'is a tibble of the right shape' is a structural check, not a test of correctness. A test that a regression coefficient on a known synthetic dataset equals the closed-form answer, or that a cell survives the pipeline unchanged, is a test of correctness. Write both, and do not mistake the first for the second. ### Integration tests on synthetic data Unit tests catch helper bugs. They do not catch bugs where the helpers work individually and their composition fails. An integration test runs the whole pipeline on a small synthetic dataset: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # inst/tinytest/test-pipeline.R # In a package the test file would load run_pipeline from R/; it is # defined here so the example executes as written. run_pipeline <- function(raw) { raw |> janitor::clean_names() |> dplyr::filter(age >= 18) |> dplyr::mutate(age_group = age_group(age)) |> tidyr::pivot_longer(dplyr::starts_with("bp_"), names_to = "visit", names_prefix = "bp_v", values_to = "bp") |> dplyr::filter(!is.na(bp)) |> dplyr::mutate(visit = as.integer(visit)) |> dplyr::select(patient_id, age_group, sex, treatment, visit, bp) } # synthetic data that exercises every branch raw <- tibble::tibble( patient_id = c(1, 2, 3, 4), age = c(25, 50, 75, 17), # one excluded bp_v1 = c(120, 140, 160, NA), bp_v2 = c(118, 138, NA, NA), sex = c("M", "F", "F", "M"), treatment = c("placebo", "active", "placebo", "active") ) clean <- run_pipeline(raw) expect_inherits(clean, "tbl_df", info = "returns a tibble") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_inherits(clean, "tbl_df", info = "returns a tibble") #> info| returns a tibble expect_equal(names(clean), c("patient_id", "age_group", "sex", "treatment", "visit", "bp"), info = "column names and order are as specified") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_equal(names(clean), c("patient_id", "age_group", "sex", #> call| "treatment", "visit", "bp"), info = "column names and order are as specified") #> info| column names and order are as specified # row count: 3 adults x 2 visits, minus NAs expect_equal(nrow(clean), 5, info = "patient 4 excluded; patient 3 has one NA bp") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_equal(nrow(clean), 5, info = "patient 4 excluded; patient 3 has one NA bp") #> info| patient 4 excluded; patient 3 has one NA bp expect_equal(clean$bp[clean$patient_id == 1 & clean$visit == 1], 120, info = "a known cell survives the pipeline unchanged") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_equal(clean$bp[clean$patient_id == 1 & clean$visit == #> call| 1], 120, info = "a known cell survives the pipeline unchanged") #> info| a known cell survives the pipeline unchanged ``` ::: The dataset has four patients and two visits, but it exercises each cleaning rule: the age exclusion (patient 4) and a missing value (patient 3, visit 2). The rule generalizes: for each filter, derivation, pivot, and recode, the fixture has at least one row that exercises it, including the branches you do not think exist. ### Reference tests For an output that is tedious to assert literally, compare it with a stored reference. The first run writes the object to a file and passes; later runs compare against it. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ref_file <- file.path(tempdir(), "lm-coefs.rds") unlink(ref_file) fit <- lm(mpg ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars) refit <- lm(mpg ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars[-1, ]) c(first_run = expect_equal_to_reference(coef(fit), ref_file), later_run = expect_equal_to_reference(coef(fit), ref_file), changed = expect_equal_to_reference(coef(refit), ref_file)) #> first_run later_run changed #> TRUE TRUE FALSE ``` ::: When a reference test fails, you decide whether the change is intended (delete the file and regenerate it) or a regression. The stored object is compared by value, so a coefficient that changed fails and a `print` method that gained a blank line does not. Inspect the reference once when it is first written, because the first run accepts whatever the code produced. | Use a reference test when | Avoid it when | |---|---| | The output is complex and tedious to assert literally | The output changes for trivial reasons: an unseeded random draw, the locale, an unstable sort | | The question is 'is this what was reviewed' | The stored object is too large to inspect when it changes, so 'accept or investigate' becomes a coin toss | : When a reference test helps. {#tbl-testing-reference} ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** Your test asserts `expect_equal(nrow(result), 100)`, and it passes. Does this mean the result is correct? **Answer.** No. It says nothing about which rows, what values, or whether the right rows were filtered; 100 rows of the wrong patients pass. Add assertions on content: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} result <- data.frame(patient_id = 1:100, age = rep(40:49, 10)) expected_ids <- 1:100 expected_ages <- rep(40:49, 10) expect_equal(nrow(result), 100) # structural #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_equal(nrow(result), 100) expect_equal(sort(result$patient_id), # correctness sort(expected_ids)) #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_equal(sort(result$patient_id), sort(expected_ids)) expect_equal(result$age, expected_ages) #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_equal(result$age, expected_ages) ``` ::: 'Looks right at the surface, wrong underneath' is the most common testing failure in data analysis, and a structural test alone is built to miss it. ::: ### Exercises 2. Write a `summarize_species()` function returning mean body mass and count per species from `palmerpenguins::penguins`. Give it one structural test and one correctness test, and say in a comment which is which and why the structural one is insufficient on its own. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(palmerpenguins) summarize_species <- function(data) { data |> dplyr::filter(!is.na(body_mass_g)) |> dplyr::group_by(species) |> dplyr::summarize(mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g), n = dplyr::n(), .groups = "drop") } # STRUCTURAL: shape only. Every line below passes even if # mean_mass is computed as a median, a sum, or the wrong column. out <- summarize_species(penguins) expect_inherits(out, "tbl_df", info = "structural: a tibble") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_inherits(out, "tbl_df", info = "structural: a tibble") #> info| structural: a tibble expect_equal(names(out), c("species", "mean_mass", "n"), info = "structural: column names") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_equal(names(out), c("species", "mean_mass", "n"), info = "structural: column names") #> info| structural: column names expect_equal(nrow(out), 3, info = "structural: one row per species") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_equal(nrow(out), 3, info = "structural: one row per species") #> info| structural: one row per species # CORRECTNESS: values the test computes independently. adelie <- penguins$body_mass_g[penguins$species == "Adelie"] expect_equal(out$mean_mass[out$species == "Adelie"], mean(adelie, na.rm = TRUE), info = "correctness: the mean is the mean") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_equal(out$mean_mass[out$species == "Adelie"], mean(adelie, #> call| na.rm = TRUE), info = "correctness: the mean is the mean") #> info| correctness: the mean is the mean expect_equal(out$n[out$species == "Adelie"], sum(!is.na(adelie)), info = "correctness: n counts non-missing") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_equal(out$n[out$species == "Adelie"], sum(!is.na(adelie)), #> call| info = "correctness: n counts non-missing") #> info| correctness: n counts non-missing ``` ::: The structural test is worth keeping, because a change in column names breaks callers. It is insufficient because every assertion in it would still pass if `mean()` were replaced by `median()`. Only the second test would fail, and only because it recomputes the answer a different way rather than comparing the function with itself. ::: ## Test smells {#sec-testing-smells} Some tests look like tests and produce only confidence. Two run below; @tbl-testing-smells lists the common kinds. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # foo ignores its argument and always returns 42. It is wrong for # every input, and the test below still passes. foo <- function(x) 42 expect_equal(foo(1), foo(1), # always passes info = "foo works") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_equal(foo(1), foo(1), info = "foo works") #> info| foo works ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} result <- 0.9 # nowhere near 0.5 expect_equal(result, 0.5, tolerance = 0.5) # passes for 0 to 1 #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_equal(result, 0.5, tolerance = 0.5) ``` ::: The tolerance example passes for any value from 0 to 1. With an expected value no larger than the tolerance, `all.equal()`, which `expect_equal()` uses, compares the absolute difference, so a tolerance of 0.5 around 0.5 accepts every proportion there is. | Smell | Example | Why it misleads | Fix | |---|---|---|---| | Tautology | `expect_equal(foo(1), foo(1))` | Compares the function with itself | Compare with a value computed another way | | Mocking the code under test | A stub `fit_model <- function(d) list()` inside the test | Tests the stub, not the function | Test the real function on a small input | | Brittle reference | `expect_equal_to_reference(do_thing(Sys.Date()), ...)` | Fails every day after the first, so failures stop being read | Remove the date, or compare stable fields | | Permissive tolerance | `expect_equal(x, 0.5, tolerance = 0.5)` | Accepts any proportion | Set the tolerance from the computation's real precision | | Placeholder | `expect_true(TRUE)` | Tests nothing | Write the test or delete the line | | Prefixed expectation | `tinytest::expect_equal(x, y)` in a test file | Not collected: the file reports zero tests, with only a message | Call `expect_equal()` without the prefix | | Shape only | `expect_equal(nrow(out), 100)` | Passes on the wrong rows | Assert values (@sec-testing-correctness) | : Test smells. Watch for them in code review. {#tbl-testing-smells} `tinytest` has no mocking facility, which makes the second smell harder to write by accident than under `testthat`'s `with_mocked_bindings()`. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** A colleague's test is `expect_equal(risk_difference(d), risk_difference(d), tolerance = 1e-8)`. They point out that the tolerance is tight. Is the test any good? **Answer.** No. It is a tautology with a tight tolerance: the expected value comes from calling the function under test, so it passes whatever the function returns. The tolerance is irrelevant. The fix is an expected value computed another way, for example the difference of two proportions worked out by hand on a ten-row fixture. ::: ### Exercises 3. Replace the tautological test, `expect_equal(foo(1), foo(1))`, with an assertion that fails against `foo <- function(x) 42` while passing against a correct implementation that doubles its argument. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} foo <- function(x) 42 # wrong for every input expect_equal(foo(1), 2, info = "foo doubles 1") #> ----- FAILED[data]: <--> #> call| expect_equal(foo(1), 2, info = "foo doubles 1") #> diff| Expected '2', got '42' #> info| foo doubles 1 expect_equal(foo(3), 6, info = "foo doubles 3") #> ----- FAILED[data]: <--> #> call| expect_equal(foo(3), 6, info = "foo doubles 3") #> diff| Expected '6', got '42' #> info| foo doubles 3 ``` ::: The fix is to assert against a value computed independently of the function, here by hand. Any assertion whose expected value comes from calling the function is circular, and no number of added cases repairs that. ::: ## Worked example: testing the HF-HOME CRF cleaner {#sec-testing-worked} The HF-HOME CRF (case report form) export, `analysis/data/raw_data/hfhome/crf_export.csv`, comes from five site systems that each write the same fields differently: Site D codes sex as `1` and `2`, Site C writes dates month first, Site E has lost the leading zeros of its patient IDs, and the site labels vary in case and spacing. The function below puts four fields into canonical form. Each site's coding lives in a lookup table passed as an argument with a default, so that the codebook is in one place and a change to it is a one-line change. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} #' Clean the site-specific fields of the HF-HOME CRF export #' #' @param raw Data frame read from `crf_export.csv`, every column #' character. #' @param site_d_sex Codes Site D uses for sex. #' @param date_formats Discharge-date format for each site. #' @return A data frame of `patient_id`, `site`, `sex`, and #' `discharge_date` in canonical form. clean_crf <- function(raw, site_d_sex = c("1" = "M", "2" = "F"), date_formats = c("Site A" = "%Y-%m-%d", "Site B" = "%Y-%m-%d", "Site C" = "%m/%d/%Y", "Site D" = "%d-%b-%Y", "Site E" = "%Y%m%d")) { site <- paste("Site", toupper(substring(trimws(raw$site), 6))) sex <- ifelse(site == "Site D", site_d_sex[raw$sex], toupper(substr(raw$sex, 1, 1))) if (!all(sex %in% c("F", "M"))) { stop("unrecognized sex code: ", paste(unique(raw$sex[!sex %in% c("F", "M")]), collapse = ", ")) } data.frame( patient_id = sprintf("%04d", as.integer(raw$patient_id)), site = site, sex = unname(sex), discharge_date = as.Date(raw$discharge_date, format = date_formats[site]) ) } ``` ::: The test file has two layers. The unit layer is a fixture with one row per site, each written the way that site writes it, and expected values worked out by hand from the codebook. The integration layer cleans the whole export and compares it with two independent records of the same patients: sex in the registration demographics and the discharge date in the baseline table. Agreement between independent sources is a check real trials run, and it needs no hand-written expectations.[^locale] [^locale]: `%b` matches English month abbreviations only in an English locale. On a machine whose `LC_TIME` is set otherwise, Site D's dates parse to `NA`, and the date tests below report it. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # inst/tinytest/test-clean-crf.R hf_dir <- Sys.getenv("HFHOME_DIR") fixture <- data.frame( patient_id = c("0005", "0001", "0012", "0010", "7"), site = c("Site A", "site b", "SITE C", " Site D", "Site E "), sex = c("F", "Male", "f", "2", "M"), discharge_date = c("2024-02-02", "2024-02-01", "02/03/2024", "05-FEB-2024", "20240209") ) out <- clean_crf(fixture) expect_equal(out$patient_id, c("0005", "0001", "0012", "0010", "0007"), info = "Site E IDs regain their leading zeros") expect_equal(out$site, paste("Site", LETTERS[1:5]), info = "site labels are normalized") expect_equal(out$sex, c("F", "M", "F", "F", "M"), info = "every site's sex coding; Site D codes 2 as F") expect_equal(out$discharge_date, as.Date(c("2024-02-02", "2024-02-01", "2024-02-03", "2024-02-05", "2024-02-09")), info = "every site's date format; Site C is month first") expect_error(clean_crf(transform(fixture, sex = "X")), pattern = "unrecognized sex code", info = "an unknown sex code stops the cleaning") crf <- read.csv(file.path(hf_dir, "crf_export.csv"), colClasses = "character", fileEncoding = "UTF-8-BOM") demographics <- read.csv(file.path(hf_dir, "demographics.csv"), colClasses = "character") baseline <- read.csv(file.path(hf_dir, "baseline.csv"), colClasses = "character") both <- merge(clean_crf(crf), demographics[c("patient_id", "sex")], by = "patient_id", suffixes = c("", "_demo")) both <- merge(both, baseline[c("patient_id", "discharge_date")], by = "patient_id", suffixes = c("", "_base")) expect_equal(nrow(both), nrow(crf), info = "every CRF patient is found in both sources") expect_equal(both$sex, both$sex_demo, info = "sex agrees with the registration record") expect_equal(both$discharge_date, as.Date(both$discharge_date_base), info = "discharge date agrees with the baseline table") ``` ::: In a project this chunk is the file `inst/tinytest/test-clean-crf.R`. The chunk below writes it to a temporary file and runs it as `tinytest` would, with the data directory passed in an environment variable rather than written into the test. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} test_file <- file.path(tempdir(), "test-clean-crf.R") writeLines(knitr::knit_code$get("test-crf-tests"), test_file) hf_env <- list( HFHOME_DIR = normalizePath(file.path("..", "data", "raw_data", "hfhome")) ) passing <- run_test_file(test_file, verbose = 0, set_env = hf_env) passing #> All ok, 8 results (100ms) ``` ::: Every test passes. That shows the tests agree with the function; it does not yet show that they would notice if the function were wrong. To find out, plant a bug a reviewer could plausibly miss, here Site D's sex codes swapped, and run the same tests again: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} clean_crf_correct <- clean_crf clean_crf <- function(raw) { clean_crf_correct(raw, site_d_sex = c("1" = "F", "2" = "M")) } mutant <- run_test_file(test_file, verbose = 0, set_env = hf_env) mutant #> ----- FAILED[data]: test-clean-crf.R<17--18> #> call| expect_equal(out$sex, c("F", "M", "F", "F", "M"), info = "every site's sex coding; Site D codes 2 as F") #> diff| 1 string mismatch #> info| every site's sex coding; Site D codes 2 as F #> ----- FAILED[data]: test-clean-crf.R<40--41> #> call| expect_equal(both$sex, both$sex_demo, info = "sex agrees with the registration record") #> diff| 373 string mismatches #> info| sex agrees with the registration record #> #> Showing 2 out of 8 results: 2 fails, 6 passes (45ms) clean_crf <- clean_crf_correct ``` ::: Both layers catch it: the fixture's Site D row, and the comparison with the registration record, which disagrees for every Site D patient. The swapped function returns a plausible data frame, with two sexes in plausible proportions, which is exactly the kind of bug that survives inspection (Habit 8). This check has a name: **mutation testing** [@demillo1978hints]. Each planted bug is a *mutant*; a test that fails on it *kills* it; and the share of mutants killed measures how much the suite can see. Tools for other languages generate mutants automatically (flipped comparisons, swapped constants, deleted lines). By hand, plant one mutant per rule in the codebook, starting with the rules whose failure would produce a plausible number. ::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'} Confirm in code that the suite passes the correct function and fails the mutant, so that a later edit to the tests cannot quietly make them blind to it. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} stopifnot(tinytest::all_pass(passing), tinytest::any_fail(mutant)) ``` ::: The chunk prints nothing when both hold. ::: ::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'} An agentic version: a coding agent writes tests and runs mutants, and you review the evidence rather than only the code. > **Context.** `R/clean_crf.R` cleans the HF-HOME CRF export. The > codebook, `analysis/data/raw_data/hfhome/README.md`, lists each > site's coding of sex, dates, IDs, and site labels. Existing tests > are in `inst/tinytest/`. Run code only against the synthetic > HF-HOME files. > > **Constraints.** Add tests in a new file, > `inst/tinytest/test-clean-crf-sites.R`. Do not edit > `R/clean_crf.R` or any existing test file, do not skip, delete, > or loosen a test, and add no packages. If a test you write fails > against the current function, stop and report it; do not change > the test to make it pass. > > **Criteria.** Before writing tests, list each codebook rule and > the fixture row that will exercise it. Then, for each rule, > create one mutant of `clean_crf()` in a temporary copy, run the > suite against it, and report a table of mutant, killed or > survived, and the test that killed it. *Failure mode.* An agent told to make tests pass will weaken them: it widens a tolerance, replaces a value check with a shape check, or edits the expected value to match the output. That is why the instruction forbids touching existing tests, and why the rule that tests are off-limits to an agent is part of the book's governance rules (@sec-ai-governance). *Check.* Run `git diff --stat -- inst/tinytest/ R/` and confirm that only the new test file changed; read every `expect_*()` in it for a hand-derived expected value; then run one mutant yourself, as in the chunk above, and confirm that the suite fails. The codebook and synthetic files hold no patient data. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** Why does the fixture have one row per site, written by hand, rather than five rows sampled from the export? **Answer.** Every pathology in the export is per site, so a test must exercise every site to exercise every branch. Five sampled rows can easily miss Site D, whose numeric sex codes are the branch most likely to be wrong, and a sample changes when the export does. A hand-built row per site exercises each branch on purpose, and its expected values come from the codebook rather than from the function. ::: ### Exercises 4. Make a second mutant that parses Site C's dates day first (`"%d/%m/%Y"`). Predict which tests kill it, run the suite, and count how many Site C dates the mutant gets silently wrong, rather than `NA`. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} day_first <- eval(formals(clean_crf_correct)$date_formats) day_first["Site C"] <- "%d/%m/%Y" clean_crf <- function(raw) { clean_crf_correct(raw, date_formats = day_first) } mutant_c <- run_test_file(test_file, verbose = 0, set_env = hf_env) mutant_c #> ----- FAILED[data]: test-clean-crf.R<19--22> #> call| expect_equal(out$discharge_date, as.Date(c("2024-02-02", "2024-02-01", #> call| --> "2024-02-03", "2024-02-05", "2024-02-09")), info = "every site's date format; Site C is month first") #> diff| Mean relative difference: 0.001417291 #> info| every site's date format; Site C is month first #> ----- FAILED[data]: test-clean-crf.R<42--43> #> call| expect_equal(both$discharge_date, as.Date(both$discharge_date_base), #> call| --> info = "discharge date agrees with the baseline table") #> diff| 'is.NA' value mismatch: 271 in current 0 in target #> info| discharge date agrees with the baseline table #> #> Showing 2 out of 8 results: 2 fails, 6 passes (41ms) crf <- read.csv(file.path(hf_env$HFHOME_DIR, "crf_export.csv"), colClasses = "character", fileEncoding = "UTF-8-BOM") right <- clean_crf_correct(crf) wrong <- clean_crf(crf) in_c <- right$site == "Site C" c(site_c = sum(in_c), became_na = sum(is.na(wrong$discharge_date[in_c])), silently_wrong = sum(!is.na(wrong$discharge_date[in_c]) & wrong$discharge_date[in_c] != right$discharge_date[in_c])) #> site_c became_na silently_wrong #> 498 271 207 clean_crf <- clean_crf_correct ``` ::: The fixture's date test and the comparison with the baseline table both kill the mutant. The counts show why the comparison matters more than it seems: dates whose day is above 12 become `NA`, which is loud, but every date whose day is 12 or below, and differs from its month, parses to a valid date in the wrong month. The third count is the one that matters: those dates pass every check except a comparison with something independent. ::: 5. The CRF's `sbp_discharge` column marks a missing value three ways: an empty field, `NA`, and `-99`. Write `clean_sbp()`, which returns numeric systolic blood pressure with every missing code as `NA`, and a test that compares it with `sbp_discharge` in `baseline.csv`. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} clean_sbp <- function(x) { x <- trimws(x) x[x %in% c("", "NA", "-99")] <- NA as.numeric(x) } crf_raw <- read.csv(file.path(hf_env$HFHOME_DIR, "crf_export.csv"), colClasses = "character", fileEncoding = "UTF-8-BOM", na.strings = character()) crf_raw$patient_id <- sprintf("%04d", as.integer(crf_raw$patient_id)) baseline <- read.csv(file.path(hf_env$HFHOME_DIR, "baseline.csv"), colClasses = c(patient_id = "character")) both <- merge(crf_raw[c("patient_id", "sbp_discharge")], baseline[c("patient_id", "sbp_discharge")], by = "patient_id", suffixes = c("_crf", "_base")) expect_equal(clean_sbp(both$sbp_discharge_crf), as.numeric(both$sbp_discharge_base), info = "every missing code becomes NA; values unchanged") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_equal(clean_sbp(both$sbp_discharge_crf), as.numeric(both$sbp_discharge_base), #> call| info = "every missing code becomes NA; values unchanged") #> info| every missing code becomes NA; values unchanged c(missing_crf = sum(is.na(clean_sbp(both$sbp_discharge_crf))), missing_baseline = sum(is.na(both$sbp_discharge_base))) #> missing_crf missing_baseline #> 78 78 ``` ::: `na.strings = character()` keeps the raw codes as text, so that the function, not `read.csv()`, decides what is missing; with the default, `NA` is converted on reading and `-99` is not, and the test would no longer exercise the function's handling of either. A version that forgot `-99` would leave impossible pressures of -99 mmHg in the data, which a mean would absorb without complaint; the comparison with the baseline table fails on it. ::: ## Running tests in continuous integration {#sec-testing-ci} Tests that run only when someone remembers to run them catch regressions late. Continuous integration (CI) runs them on every push; @sec-ci covers it in full. For an R package, `usethis::use_github_action("check-standard")` sets up GitHub Actions to run `R CMD check`, which runs the tests, on several operating systems and R versions. For an analysis project, the equivalent is a workflow that runs the tests. It assumes a `DESCRIPTION` file listing the project's dependencies, as a research compendium has; without one, replace `local::.` with the packages the tests need: ```yaml # .github/workflows/test.yaml name: tests on: [push, pull_request] jobs: test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2 - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r-dependencies@v2 with: packages: | local::. any::tinytest - name: Run tests run: | Rscript -e 'res <- tinytest::test_all()' \ -e 'quit(status = as.integer(tinytest::any_fail(res)))' ``` ::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'} **A green CI job can contain failing tests.** The second `-e` line is not optional. `tinytest::test_all()` reports failures but returns normally, so `Rscript` exits with status 0 and the job stays green however many tests fail. A CI step fails only on a nonzero exit status, so the script must turn 'any test failed' into one. ::: ::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'} Run a one-test suite that fails, in a fresh R process as CI would, with and without the `quit()` line, and compare the exit statuses. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} failing <- file.path(tempdir(), "failing-suite") dir.create(failing, showWarnings = FALSE) writeLines("expect_equal(1 + 1, 3)", file.path(failing, "test-fail.R")) r_libs <- paste0("R_LIBS=", paste(.libPaths(), collapse = .Platform$path.sep)) rscript <- function(...) { system2(file.path(R.home("bin"), "Rscript"), shQuote(c("--vanilla", ...)), env = r_libs, stdout = FALSE, stderr = FALSE) } run_suite <- sprintf("res <- tinytest::run_test_dir('%s')", failing) c(without_quit = rscript("-e", run_suite), with_quit = rscript("-e", run_suite, "-e", "quit(status = as.integer(tinytest::any_fail(res)))")) #> without_quit with_quit #> 0 1 ``` ::: Status 0 is what CI reads as success. Only the version with `quit()` reports the failing test as a failure. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** A teammate's workflow runs `Rscript -e 'tinytest::test_all()'` and has been green for a month. What do you know about the tests? **Answer.** Only that the R process started and `test_all()` returned. Without the `quit(status = ...)` line, a run in which every test failed also exits with status 0. Open the log of the latest run and read the summary line, then add the `quit()` line and push a deliberately failing test to see the job turn red. ::: ## For testthat readers {#sec-testing-testthat} `testthat` is the framework you are most likely to meet elsewhere, and where a project already depends on it, stay with it; mixing frameworks in one suite buys nothing. The discipline of this chapter is the same under either, and most of the translation is mechanical (@tbl-testing-testthat). | `tinytest` | `testthat` | |---|---| | `expect_equal(x, y, info = "...")` at the top level of the file | `test_that("...", { expect_equal(x, y) })` | | `expect_inherits(x, "tbl_df")` | `expect_s3_class(x, "tbl_df")` | | `expect_equal(names(x), c(...))` | `expect_named(x, c(...))` | | `expect_equal(sort(a), sort(b))` | `expect_setequal(a, b)` | | `expect_equal_to_reference(x, "ref.rds")`, stores the object | `expect_snapshot()`, stores printed output; `expect_snapshot_value()`, stores the value | | `tinysnapshot::expect_snapshot_plot(p, "label")` | `vdiffr::expect_doppelganger("label", p)` | | `run_test_file()`, `test_all()` | `test_file()`, `devtools::test()` | : The same tests in both frameworks. {#tbl-testing-testthat} `tinytest`'s missing functions are a choice rather than a gap: each is a plain comparison whose failure prints the two values. Visual regression testing of `ggplot2` output is the one place the two ecosystems differ in maturity. `vdiffr`, which stores an SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics) file of the plot and compares later renders with it, runs only inside `testthat`; `tinysnapshot` is the `tinytest` equivalent, younger and less widely used. ## Rules of thumb 1. **Habit 9: test the statistics, not the shape.** Every test file needs at least one assertion against a value computed another way: by hand, in closed form, or from an independent source. 2. **Habit 8: plant the bug before you trust the test.** A suite you have never seen fail has not shown that it can; run one mutant per codebook rule. 3. **Habit 3: version control from day one.** Run the tests in CI on every push, with an exit status that turns red when any test fails. ## Cumulative practice 6. *Cumulative (uses @sec-git-teams).* Review a colleague's test suite rather than their code. For each test, decide whether it checks statistical content or only structure, and find at least one test that would pass even if the function under test were subtly wrong. Write the mutant that survives, propose the value-level assertion that kills it, and deliver the review as a pull-request comment. 7. *On your own work (no key).* Add unit tests for two functions from an analysis of yours (a typical case, an edge case, and an error), an integration test on a synthetic fixture that exercises every branch, and a CI workflow that runs them. Plant one mutant and confirm that the suite, and the CI job, turn red. ## Cheat sheet | Task | Code | Guards against | |---|---|---| | Assert a value | `expect_equal(f(x), expected, info = "...")` | A function that returns the wrong number | | Assert an error | `expect_error(f(bad), pattern = "...")` | Bad input passing silently | | Assert a class | `expect_inherits(x, "data.frame")` | A changed return type | | Compare with a stored object | `expect_equal_to_reference(x, "ref.rds")` | Unreviewed changes to complex output | | Run one file | `run_test_file("test-x.R", set_env = list(...))` | Tests that depend on the working directory | | Run every test | `tinytest::test_all()` | Untested corners of the project | | Fail CI on a failed test | `quit(status = as.integer(any_fail(res)))` | A green job with failing tests | | Check the tests can see a bug | Plant a mutant; `any_fail(res)` | A suite that passes everything | : Testing at a glance. {#tbl-testing-cheat-sheet} ## Further reading - [@wickham2023rpkgs], the testing chapters, the canonical `testthat` reference, whose advice on designing a suite applies under either framework. - The `tinytest` vignette, `vignette('using_tinytest', package = 'tinytest')`, the reference for the framework this chapter uses. - [@demillo1978hints], the paper that introduced mutation analysis as a way to judge test data. ## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-20} 1. Even a one-off analysis benefits from tests: they catch regressions when you refactor mid-analysis, they serve as executable documentation of expected behavior, and they detect silent failures when upstream data change format. The cost of writing a handful of tests is small; the cost of silently mis-analyzing data is much larger. 2. A unit test exercises a single function with known inputs and checks the output. An integration test runs a pipeline segment (multiple functions) on synthetic data and checks the pipeline's output. An end-to-end test runs the full analysis pipeline from raw data to final figures and tables. Unit tests are fast and narrow; end-to-end tests are slow and broad; integration tests sit in between, with good cost-benefit for analytic pipelines. 3. `expect_equal_to_reference()` captures the *object* an expression returns (a coefficient vector, a fitted summary, a data frame) by saving it to an `.rds` file on first run, when the test passes trivially. On subsequent runs it compares the new object against the saved one, so it detects changed values but ignores changes in how they print. Use it when the output is complex and not easily expressed as a literal value. Inspect the stored reference once, since the first run accepts whatever the code produced, and review every later difference manually before deleting and regenerating the file.
